planting.note: Set out plugs or container plants in spring once soil can be worked; full sun brings out the darkest foliage color and best bloom.

directions: Plant divisions or nursery plugs in spring into average, well-drained garden soil, spacing them a foot or so apart to let the spreading mat fill in within a season or two. Give Midnight Mystery full sun for the deepest near-black foliage and heaviest rosy-pink spring flower spikes, though it will tolerate light shade with somewhat less color intensity. Keep new plantings evenly moist until established and ensure good air movement around the crowns, since dense, humid conditions can invite crown or powdery mildew issues. Once settled, this semi-evergreen groundcover needs little beyond an occasional edge trim to keep it from wandering into lawn areas.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall; afternoon shade protects flowers and foliage from winter sun scald in colder parts of its range.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil, siting them where they get morning sun but afternoon shade to protect the flowers from scorching. This vernalis hybrid carries a graceful, semi-weeping branch habit and opens carmine-red blooms edged in white from fall into winter, peaking right around the holiday season. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and avoid heavy fertilizing in late summer, which can push soft growth vulnerable to early cold snaps. Prune lightly right after bloom finishes if shaping is needed, since next year's buds form on the current season's wood.

common_name: Key Lime Lamb's Ear (Chartreuse Fuzzy-Leaved Betony)

planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring into lean, fast-draining soil; this selection, a sport of 'Big Ears' found in Georgia, holds its chartreuse color and dense felted texture better than older lamb's ear cultivars in humid summer heat.

directions: Set container plants or rooted divisions in spring into lean, well-drained to average soil, spacing them two to three feet apart to leave room for the wide-spreading, extra-fuzzy chartreuse mat. Full sun keeps the thick, felted leaves brightest and helps the clump resist the crown rot that can plague lamb's ear in damp, heavy soils. Shear off the purple summer flower spikes if a tidier, all-foliage look is preferred, or leave them for pollinators. Water sparingly once established, since Key Lime tolerates dry conditions far better than wet feet.

common_name: Fruit Snacks All Red Apple (Red-Fleshed Columnar Apple)
scientific_name: Malus domestica 'Fruit Snacks All Red' (UEB 4772/1) PPAF

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring once soil can be worked; site a compatible apple pollinator within range since this columnar selection does not reliably self-pollinate. Distinct from the already-grown 'Tasty Red' Fruit Snacks apple (UEB 3449-1) by its different breeding code and red-fleshed, not just red-skinned, fruit.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, setting trees roughly two feet apart if growing several in a hedge-like row along a fence or patio edge. This columnar apple is unusual for carrying red color all the way through the flesh rather than just the skin, giving tart, waxy fruit that resists browning once cut and makes a striking addition to salads or baked goods. Because the narrow, upright habit needs minimal pruning, just remove dead, crossing, or inward-growing wood in late winter. Plant a second apple variety blooming at the same time nearby to ensure good cross-pollination and reliable yields.

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container nursery stock in spring; the narrow habit and Japanese-beetle resistance suit it well to street tree and urban boulevard plantings.

directions: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown nursery stock in spring into average garden or urban soil, watering deeply through the first two seasons while the root system establishes. This Tilia americana x T. tomentosa 'Petiolaris' hybrid, collected from Kornik Gardens, Poland in the 1930s-40s and named by the Morton Arboretum for its 100th anniversary, forms a relatively narrow canopy valued for street tree and boulevard plantings where wider lindens won't fit. Clusters of small, intensely fragrant cream flowers open in mid- to late June and draw heavy honeybee traffic. Its glossy deep green foliage shows notably better resistance to Japanese beetle skeletonizing than many other linden species.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall into consistently moist, well-drained soil; adaptable to sun, part shade, or shade. A natural mutation of 'Feather Falls' discovered in Zebulon, NC in 2020; won a Retailers' Choice Award at Cultivate'26.

directions: Plant container divisions in spring or fall into moist, well-drained soil, and expect this vigorous evergreen sedge to settle in quickly with minimal care once established. Its arching blades carry wide, bright white margins against green centers, giving the clump a luminous, two-tone glow that holds up through winter in mild climates. Lunar Falls adapts to full sun, part shade, or fairly deep shade, making it a flexible choice for woodland edges, container combinations, or mixed perennial borders. Trim back tattered winter foliage in early spring before new growth emerges to keep the clump looking fresh.
sources: Garden Center magazine -- Cultivate'26 award coverage

common_name: Jolly Hearts Spark Bleeding Heart (Golden-Leaved Red-Veined Dicentra)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to part shade; the plant dies back and goes dormant by midsummer like other old-fashioned bleeding hearts. Part of a registered series alongside 'Love' (17001GR1) and 'Crush' (17001BDP1).

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in a shaded or semi-shaded woodland bed. Jolly Hearts Spark pairs golden-yellow foliage threaded with striking red veins against deep red, heart-shaped flowers dangling from gracefully arching stems in mid- to late spring. Keep the soil from drying out during the bloom period, since this old-fashioned bleeding heart will decline and go summer-dormant faster under drought stress. Once dormant, let the foliage die back naturally and mark the spot, since nothing will show above ground again until the following spring.
